title: Respiratory I: Physiology and Pulmonary Function
summary: Ventilation, gas exchange and how lung function is measured.

lessons.title: Lung Anatomy and Mechanics

levels.kid:
Your lungs are like two big sponges in your chest. They are full of tiny air bubbles called alveoli.

Air goes in through your nose and mouth, down a big tube called the windpipe, and then into smaller and smaller tubes, like the branches of an upside-down tree.

A big flat muscle under your lungs, the diaphragm, pulls down when you breathe in. That makes more room in your chest, so air rushes in, like when you pull open a squeezy bottle. When the muscle relaxes, the stretchy lungs spring back and push the air out, like a balloon letting go.

Breathing in takes work. Breathing out at rest is free!
levels.hs:
The respiratory system has two parts. The **conducting zone** (nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles) warms, humidifies and filters air but does no gas exchange. This is called **anatomic dead space**. The **respiratory zone** (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and about 300-500 million **alveoli**) is where oxygen and carbon dioxide cross into and out of the blood.

Breathing in (inspiration) is **active**. The **diaphragm** contracts and moves down, and the external intercostal muscles lift the ribs. The chest gets bigger, pressure inside the lungs drops slightly below air pressure, and air flows in.

Breathing out (expiration) at rest is **passive**: the lungs and chest wall recoil elastically. During exercise or coughing, the abdominal and internal intercostal muscles help push air out.

Two properties shape how easy breathing is:
- **Compliance:** how easily the lungs stretch. Stiff lungs (scarring) have low compliance.
- **Airway resistance:** how hard it is to push air through the tubes. Narrow airways (asthma) have high resistance.

**Surfactant**, made by type II alveolar cells, lowers surface tension so tiny alveoli do not collapse. Premature babies who lack it can develop breathing trouble called respiratory distress syndrome.
levels.college:
Air flows down a pressure gradient. At rest between breaths, alveolar pressure equals atmospheric pressure and **intrapleural pressure** is negative (about −5 cmH2O), because the lung's inward elastic recoil and the chest wall's outward recoil pull the pleural layers apart. **Transpulmonary pressure** (alveolar minus intrapleural) is the distending pressure that keeps alveoli open. A pneumothorax abolishes the negative pleural pressure, so the lung collapses inward and the chest wall springs out.

**Compliance** = ΔV/ΔP. It is reduced in pulmonary fibrosis, edema, ARDS and loss of surfactant, and increased in emphysema (loss of elastic tissue), where recoil is weak and air is trapped. **Functional residual capacity (FRC)** is the volume at which lung and chest-wall recoil balance.

**Surface tension**: by Laplace's law (P = 2T/r), small alveoli would empty into large ones; surfactant (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine-rich) lowers tension more as alveoli shrink, stabilizing them and reducing the work of breathing.

**Resistance**: by Poiseuille's relationship, resistance rises with the fourth power of falling radius. Most resistance sits in the medium-sized bronchi, not the tiny bronchioles, because the bronchioles are arranged in vast parallel. Resistance falls at higher lung volumes, which tug airways open (radial traction). In **forced expiration**, rising pleural pressure compresses airways at the equal pressure point; in emphysema, lost traction moves this point upstream and airways collapse early, which is why patients purse their lips.

**Dead space**: anatomic (conducting airways, roughly 150 mL in an adult) plus alveolar (ventilated but unperfused alveoli) equals physiologic dead space. Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead space) × respiratory rate, so rapid shallow breathing wastes ventilation.
levels.phd:
Lung mechanics are classically described by the equation of motion of the respiratory system: Pressure applied = (Volume / Compliance) + (Flow × Resistance) + inertance, with inertance negligible at normal frequencies. Elastic work is stored during inspiration and returned during passive expiration; resistive work is dissipated as heat. The pressure-volume curve of an isolated lung shows **hysteresis**: inflation and deflation follow different paths, largely because surfactant behaves differently on expansion versus compression and because recruitment of collapsed units needs higher opening pressures than keeping them open.

Surfactant is about 90% lipid and 10% protein. Surfactant proteins B and C are hydrophobic and promote rapid adsorption and film spreading; SP-A and SP-D are collectins with innate immune roles. Inherited SP-B deficiency is lethal in neonates, and SP-C and ABCA3 variants cause childhood interstitial lung disease, linking surfactant biology to fibrosis.

Regional heterogeneity matters. Gravity makes pleural pressure less negative at the base, so in an upright person apical alveoli are more inflated at FRC but basal alveoli sit on a steeper part of their compliance curve and receive more ventilation per breath. Time constants (τ = R × C) vary between units; units with long time constants fill and empty slowly, producing pendelluft and frequency dependence of dynamic compliance, an early marker of small airway disease.

The **wave-speed theory of flow limitation** explains why maximal expiratory flow becomes effort-independent: flow cannot exceed the speed at which a pressure wave travels in the compliant airway wall, set by airway area and wall stiffness. This underpins the shape of the flow-volume loop.

At the alveolar level, interdependence (each alveolus tethered by neighbors) resists focal collapse, and loss of this tethering contributes to heterogeneous strain in injured lungs, a concept central to ventilator-induced lung injury.
levels.expert:
At the bedside you rarely calculate compliance from first principles, but you constantly reason with it. On a mechanically ventilated patient, two numbers do most of the work:
- **Peak pressure** reflects resistance plus elastance.
- **Plateau pressure** (measured during an inspiratory hold, no flow) reflects elastance alone.

A rising peak with a stable plateau means a resistance problem: kinked or bitten tube, secretions, mucus plug, bronchospasm. Rising peak and plateau together mean compliance has fallen: pneumothorax, mainstem intubation, pulmonary edema, worsening ARDS, abdominal distension. That single split sorts the emergency differential within seconds.

**Driving pressure** (plateau minus PEEP) is effectively tidal volume divided by compliance, and lower driving pressure is associated with better survival in ARDS. Lung-protective ventilation keeps tidal volume low relative to predicted body weight and plateau pressure limited; obese patients and those with tense abdomens have a stiff chest wall, so an esophageal balloon can separate lung from chest-wall mechanics when this matters.

In the awake patient, signs of increased work of breathing are the clinical readout of mechanics: tachypnea, accessory muscle use, tracheal tug, paradoxical abdominal movement (diaphragm fatigue or paralysis), and the inability to speak in full sentences. A rising PaCO2 in a tiring asthmatic is an ominous sign, not a reassuring 'normal' value.

In severe COPD watch for **dynamic hyperinflation and auto-PEEP**: incomplete exhalation stacks breaths, raises intrathoracic pressure, impairs venous return and can cause hypotension right after intubation. The fix is to allow longer expiratory time (slower rate, lower tidal volume) and, in a crisis, briefly disconnect the ventilator.

For neurosurgery: cord injury at or above C3-C5, the phrenic nerve roots, paralyzes the diaphragm, and positioning changes, including prone spine surgery, alter chest-wall compliance.

keyPoints: The conducting zone is dead space; alveoli exchange gas
Inspiration is active (diaphragm); quiet expiration is passive recoil
Intrapleural pressure is normally negative
Compliance is low in fibrosis and high in emphysema
Surfactant from type II cells prevents alveolar collapse

lessons.title: Gas Exchange and V/Q Matching

levels.kid:
Inside your lungs, every tiny air bubble is wrapped in super tiny blood tubes. The bubble wall is so thin that oxygen can slip right through into the blood, and the waste gas, carbon dioxide, slips out to be breathed away. It is like passing notes through a very thin curtain.

For this to work well, two things must match: air coming into a bubble and blood flowing past it. Air with no blood is wasted. Blood with no air goes back to the body without picking up oxygen.

Your lungs are clever. They try to send blood to the bubbles that are getting the most air.
levels.hs:
Gas exchange happens by **diffusion**: gases move from where their pressure (partial pressure) is high to where it is low.
- In the alveoli, oxygen pressure is high and carbon dioxide is low.
- In blood arriving from the body, oxygen is low and carbon dioxide is high.
So oxygen moves into the blood and carbon dioxide moves out.

The barrier is extremely thin (well under a thousandth of a millimetre) and has a huge surface area, about the size of a tennis court. Diffusion is slower if the barrier thickens (scarring) or the surface area shrinks (emphysema).

Most oxygen in blood is carried bound to **hemoglobin** in red blood cells; only a tiny amount dissolves in plasma. Carbon dioxide is carried mostly as **bicarbonate**.

**V/Q matching** compares ventilation (V, air reaching alveoli) with perfusion (Q, blood flow). The ideal is a balance. Two extremes:
- **Dead space:** air but no blood (for example, a clot blocking a lung artery). V/Q is very high.
- **Shunt:** blood but no air (for example, alveoli filled with pus in pneumonia). V/Q is zero.

The lung protects matching through **hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction**: lung arteries near poorly ventilated alveoli squeeze down, redirecting blood to better areas. This is the opposite of how arteries elsewhere in the body react to low oxygen.
levels.college:
**Fick's law**: diffusion rate ∝ (area × diffusion coefficient × partial pressure gradient) / thickness. CO2 is about 20 times more soluble than O2, so it diffuses far more readily; hypercapnia from diffusion impairment essentially does not occur.

Normally capillary blood reaches alveolar PO2 within about the first third of its transit time (about 0.75 s at rest). This reserve means diffusion problems typically cause hypoxemia only during exercise, when transit time shortens, or at altitude, when the gradient is smaller.

Gases are perfusion-limited (equilibrate fast, so uptake rises only with more blood flow; O2 normally behaves this way) or diffusion-limited (never equilibrate; carbon monoxide). CO's diffusion limitation is why it is used to measure **DLCO**.

**V/Q**: the overall ratio is about 0.8 (alveolar ventilation roughly 4 L/min, cardiac output about 5 L/min). In the upright lung both ventilation and perfusion increase toward the base, but perfusion increases more steeply, so V/Q is highest at the apex (about 3) and lowest at the base (about 0.6). Consequences: apical alveolar PO2 is highest, which favors reactivation tuberculosis there.

Low V/Q units deliver blood with low PO2 and somewhat high PCO2. Because the oxyhemoglobin curve is flat at the top, high V/Q units cannot add extra O2 to compensate, so mixed blood stays hypoxemic. CO2 behaves differently: its dissociation curve is nearly linear, and increased overall ventilation corrects PCO2. This is why V/Q mismatch typically produces hypoxemia with a normal or low PaCO2.

V/Q mismatch responds well to supplemental oxygen; a true shunt responds poorly because shunted blood never meets the enriched gas.
levels.phd:
The **three-compartment model** (Riley and Cournand) collapses the lung's continuous V/Q distribution into ideal, dead-space and shunt compartments, from which venous admixture and physiological dead space (Bohr-Enghoff) are computed. The **multiple inert gas elimination technique** (MIGET), developed by Wagner and West, infuses six inert gases of differing solubility and recovers a near-continuous V/Q distribution, showing, for example, bimodal high-V/Q modes in emphysema and low-V/Q modes in asthma that are not visible in global indices.

Oxygen transport follows the **oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve**, whose sigmoid shape reflects cooperative binding between the T (tense) and R (relaxed) states of hemoglobin. Rightward shifts (raised temperature, PCO2, H+, and 2,3-BPG) lower affinity and favor unloading in tissue; the **Bohr effect** links pH and CO2 to affinity, while the **Haldane effect** describes deoxygenated hemoglobin binding more CO2 and H+. Carbonic anhydrase in red cells and the chloride shift (band 3, AE1) make bicarbonate the dominant CO2 carrier.

Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is intrinsic to pulmonary artery smooth muscle: alveolar hypoxia alters mitochondrial redox signaling and reactive oxygen species, inhibits voltage-gated potassium channels, depolarizes cells and opens L-type calcium channels. It is biphasic, and global alveolar hypoxia, as at altitude, causes diffuse vasoconstriction, pulmonary hypertension and, in susceptible people, high-altitude pulmonary edema from uneven overperfusion.

The West zones describe interplay of alveolar, arterial and venous pressures: zone 1 (alveolar > arterial, no flow, rarely present unless hypotension or high airway pressure), zone 2 (flow set by arterial minus alveolar, the 'waterfall'), and zone 3 (arterial minus venous). Positive-pressure ventilation can expand zone 1 and dead space, which is visible in a falling end-tidal CO2.
levels.expert:
Practical V/Q thinking guides daily decisions.

**Response to oxygen is a diagnostic test.** Hypoxemia that corrects readily with modest supplemental oxygen suggests V/Q mismatch (COPD, asthma, early pneumonia, PE). Hypoxemia refractory to high inspired oxygen suggests shunt: dense consolidation, ARDS, lobar collapse, or an intracardiac or intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt (consider a bubble echo for a patent foramen ovale or hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia).

**Positioning is V/Q therapy.** In unilateral lung disease, place the good lung down ('good lung down') so gravity sends more blood to the better-ventilated lung. Prone positioning in moderate-to-severe ARDS recruits dorsal lung, makes ventilation more even and improves survival when started early and maintained for long sessions.

**Watch HPV get overridden.** Systemic vasodilators can blunt hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and worsen oxygenation in pneumonia or COPD. Inhaled vasodilators act only in ventilated regions and can improve matching, which is why inhaled nitric oxide is used as a rescue in some severe hypoxemia, though without proven mortality benefit in ARDS.

**End-tidal CO2 versus arterial CO2.** A widening gap signals increased dead space: PE, hypovolemia, low cardiac output or overdistension. A sudden fall in end-tidal CO2 in an intubated patient can be a massive PE or cardiac arrest, not just a disconnection.

**Oxygen in chronic hypercapnia.** In some COPD patients, high-flow oxygen raises PaCO2 mainly by releasing HPV in poorly ventilated units (worsening V/Q) and through the Haldane effect, more than by suppressing drive. Target a saturation of 88-92% in at-risk patients.

Neurosurgical relevance: neurogenic pulmonary edema after subarachnoid hemorrhage or severe head injury creates shunt and can be abrupt.

keyPoints: Gases diffuse down partial pressure gradients (Fick's law)
O2 rides on hemoglobin; CO2 travels mostly as bicarbonate
Dead space = air without blood; shunt = blood without air
V/Q is highest at the apex, lowest at the base
Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts blood to ventilated lung

lessons.title: Causes of Hypoxemia

levels.kid:
Hypoxemia is a big word that means there is not enough oxygen in the blood.

There are a few ways this can happen:
- The air itself has less oxygen, like high up on a mountain.
- You breathe too slowly or too little, like when someone is very sick and sleepy.
- The bubble walls get thick, so oxygen has trouble getting through.
- Air and blood do not meet in the same places.

Doctors check oxygen with a little clip on your finger. It shines a light through your finger and tells how full of oxygen your blood is. Then they work like detectives to find which reason it is.
levels.hs:
**Hypoxemia** means a low level of oxygen in arterial blood (low PaO2). **Hypoxia** means not enough oxygen reaching tissues; it can happen even with normal PaO2, for example with severe anemia.

There are five classic causes of hypoxemia:
- **Low inspired oxygen:** high altitude, where air pressure (and so oxygen pressure) is lower.
- **Hypoventilation:** breathing too little, so carbon dioxide builds up and pushes oxygen out of the alveoli. Causes include too much sedating medicine, brain injury, neuromuscular weakness and severe obesity.
- **Diffusion impairment:** a thickened or damaged barrier, as in lung scarring.
- **V/Q mismatch:** the most common cause overall, seen in asthma, COPD and pulmonary embolism.
- **Shunt:** blood passes completely unventilated alveoli, as in pneumonia, fluid-filled lungs, or a hole between the heart's chambers.

Doctors measure oxygen in two main ways. **Pulse oximetry** (SpO2) is a quick finger clip. An **arterial blood gas** (ABG) measures PaO2 and PaCO2 directly from an artery.

Two clues sort the causes:
- Is the carbon dioxide high? That points to hypoventilation.
- Does extra oxygen fix it easily? Shunt responds poorly; the others respond better.

Note that pulse oximeters can be less accurate in some situations, including carbon monoxide poisoning and, studies show, in people with darker skin.
levels.college:
The key tool is the **alveolar gas equation**: PAO2 = FiO2 × (Patm − PH2O) − PaCO2/R. At sea level on room air: 0.21 × (760 − 47) − 40/0.8 ≈ 150 − 50 = 100 mmHg.

The **A-a gradient** (PAO2 − PaO2) separates causes:
- **Normal A-a gradient** (lungs exchange gas normally): low FiO2 (altitude) and hypoventilation. Hypoventilation is recognized by a raised PaCO2.
- **Raised A-a gradient** (a problem inside the lung): diffusion impairment, V/Q mismatch and shunt.

A normal A-a gradient is roughly under 10-15 mmHg in young adults and rises with age (a common estimate is age/4 + 4).

Then the oxygen response test:
- V/Q mismatch and diffusion limitation improve substantially with supplemental oxygen.
- Shunt improves little once the shunt fraction is large (above roughly 30%), because shunted blood never contacts alveolar gas.

Example: a patient with opioid-induced respiratory depression has PaCO2 70 mmHg and PaO2 55 mmHg on room air. PAO2 ≈ 150 − 70/0.8 ≈ 62.5, so A-a ≈ 7.5: pure hypoventilation. If the same patient aspirates, the gradient widens.

**Tissue hypoxia** has four types: hypoxemic (low PaO2), anemic (low hemoglobin or carbon monoxide), stagnant/circulatory (low cardiac output, shock), and histotoxic (cells cannot use O2, e.g. cyanide). Oxygen delivery = cardiac output × arterial O2 content, where content ≈ 1.34 × Hb × SaO2 + 0.003 × PaO2. This explains why hemoglobin and cardiac output matter as much as PaO2.

Carbon monoxide gives a falsely normal SpO2 on standard oximeters because carboxyhemoglobin absorbs light like oxyhemoglobin; co-oximetry is needed. Methemoglobinemia drives SpO2 toward about 85% regardless of true saturation.
levels.phd:
The alveolar gas equation is a mass balance assuming steady state, an R of about 0.8 and equal inspired and expired nitrogen; its full form includes a correction term FiO2 × (1 − R)/R that matters at high FiO2. At high FiO2 the A-a gradient widens even in healthy lungs, which is why the PaO2/FiO2 ratio or the oxygenation index is preferred in critical care, though both vary with FiO2 and PEEP in shunt-dominated disease.

Shunt and V/Q mismatch lie on a continuum. Iso-shunt diagrams (Benatar, Nunn) plot PaO2 against FiO2 for given shunt fractions and show the near-flat response once shunt exceeds about 30%. The Berggren equation (Qs/Qt = (CcO2 − CaO2)/(CcO2 − CvO2)) quantifies venous admixture and exposes the role of mixed venous oxygen content: a fall in cardiac output lowers CvO2 and so worsens PaO2 for the same shunt, coupling circulation to apparent lung function.

Diffusion limitation is mainly a conceptual cause at rest; detailed modeling (Piiper, Scheid) shows that at sea level even marked barrier thickening rarely prevents end-capillary equilibrium unless transit time is shortened by exercise or pulmonary vascular loss. Much hypoxemia attributed to diffusion in interstitial disease is actually V/Q heterogeneity; diffusion contributes mostly during exercise.

Pulse oximetry rests on the Beer-Lambert law at two wavelengths (about 660 and 940 nm) and empirically calibrated ratios. Calibration cohorts historically underrepresented darker skin, producing occult hypoxemia (true SaO2 below 88% with SpO2 of 92-96%) more often in Black patients, a bias with documented effects on treatment eligibility.

Hypoxemia also triggers systemic responses: carotid body glomus cells sense low PaO2 via oxygen-sensitive potassium channels and mitochondrial signaling, driving ventilation, while HIF-mediated transcription raises erythropoietin over days. Chronic exposure remodels these pathways.
levels.expert:
The bedside approach to a hypoxemic patient is fast and structured.

**First, treat and check the reading.** Apply oxygen, look at the waveform, warm the finger, and confirm with an ABG when in doubt. Do not chase a number before you assess airway, breathing and circulation.

**Then ask three questions:**
- Is PaCO2 high? Hypercapnia means inadequate ventilation: drive (sedation, stroke, raised intracranial pressure), pump (Guillain-Barré, myasthenia, high cord injury, chest wall) or load (severe COPD or asthma). Pure hypoventilation responds to correcting the ventilation, not just to oxygen; oxygen alone can mask rising CO2.
- Is the A-a gradient wide? Then the problem is in the lung parenchyma, airways or vessels.
- Does it correct with oxygen? Refractory hypoxemia means shunt; look for consolidation, collapse, ARDS, pulmonary edema or an anatomical shunt.

**Use the chest X-ray as a sorting hat:**
- Clear film plus hypoxemia: PE, asthma or COPD, intracardiac shunt, early pneumocystis, or hepatopulmonary syndrome (worse upright: platypnea-orthodeoxia).
- White-out on one side: check the trachea. Shifted away = effusion or pneumothorax; pulled toward = collapse.
- Bilateral infiltrates: edema (cardiac versus ARDS), infection, hemorrhage.

**Pitfalls attendings see:**
- A 'normal' SpO2 in carbon monoxide poisoning.
- Silent hypoxemia (low saturation with little distress), seen in COVID-19 pneumonia.
- Treating every postoperative desaturation as pain: check for atelectasis, opioid hypoventilation, PE and aspiration.

In neurocritical care hypoxemia and hypercapnia both raise intracranial pressure (hypercapnia by cerebral vasodilation), so a brain-injured patient's oxygenation and ventilation are targets in themselves, not just numbers.

keyPoints: Five causes: low FiO2, hypoventilation, diffusion, V/Q mismatch, shunt
High PaCO2 = hypoventilation
Normal A-a gradient: altitude and hypoventilation
Shunt responds poorly to oxygen
CO poisoning gives falsely normal SpO2

kidTest.q: Breathing too slowly can make oxygen:
kidTest.explain: Less breathing means less fresh air.

kidTest.q: Name the gas that is too low in hypoxemia.
kidTest.explain: Hypoxemia = low oxygen.

kidTest.q: Doctors finding the reason are like:
kidTest.explain: They look for clues.

advancedTest.q: Room air, sea level: PaCO2 80 mmHg, PaO2 45 mmHg (R = 0.8). Interpretation?
advancedTest.explain: PAO2 ≈ 150 − 100 = 50; A-a ≈ 5, normal. Hypoventilation explains it.

advancedTest.q: Hypoxemia worse when sitting up than lying down (orthodeoxia) in a patient with cirrhosis suggests:
advancedTest.explain: Intrapulmonary vascular dilations at the bases worsen shunting upright.

advancedTest.q: Falling cardiac output worsens PaO2 for the same shunt fraction because:
choices: Mixed venous O2 content falls, so shunted blood is more desaturated
advancedTest.explain: Lower CvO2 drags down arterial content when admixed.

advancedTest.q: Why can pulse oximetry miss hypoxemia in some patients with darker skin?
choices: Calibration studies underrepresented darker skin, overestimating saturation
advancedTest.explain: Occult hypoxemia occurs more often; confirm with ABG when it matters.

lessons.title: Pulmonary Function Tests

levels.kid:
Doctors have a cool test to see how strong and open your lungs are. You take the biggest breath you can, then blow out as hard and fast as you can into a tube, like blowing out all the candles on a giant birthday cake.

A machine measures how much air you blew and how fast it came out.

If the tubes in your lungs are narrow, the air comes out slowly, like squeezing a juice box through a skinny straw. If the lungs are stiff and small, less air fits in at all, like a balloon that will not stretch.

The test helps doctors know what kind of lung trouble someone has.
levels.hs:
**Pulmonary function tests (PFTs)** measure how well the lungs move air and exchange gas.

**Spirometry** is the main test. The patient breathes in fully, then blows out as hard and fast as possible. Key numbers:
- **FVC** (forced vital capacity): the total air blown out.
- **FEV1**: the air blown out in the first second.
- **FEV1/FVC ratio**: normally about 0.75-0.8 in adults.

Two main patterns:
- **Obstructive** (asthma, COPD): narrowed airways slow the air, so FEV1 drops much more than FVC and the **ratio is low** (below 0.7).
- **Restrictive** (lung scarring, chest wall problems, weak muscles): the lungs hold less air, so both FEV1 and FVC drop and the **ratio is normal or high**.

To confirm restriction, doctors measure **total lung capacity (TLC)**, the air in the lungs after a full breath in. It is low in restriction.

Doctors also repeat spirometry after an inhaled bronchodilator. A big improvement suggests asthma, which is often reversible; COPD improves less.

**DLCO** (diffusing capacity) measures how easily gas crosses into the blood. It is low in emphysema and scarring, and normal in asthma.

Lung volumes have names: **tidal volume** (a normal breath, about half a litre), **residual volume** (air left after blowing out fully), and **functional residual capacity** (air left after a normal breath out).
levels.college:
**Interpretation in steps:**
- **Quality:** acceptable, repeatable maneuvers; poor effort mimics restriction.
- **Obstruction:** FEV1/FVC below the lower limit of normal (LLN), or below 0.70 in many COPD definitions. The fixed 0.70 cutoff overdiagnoses obstruction in older adults and underdiagnoses it in the young. Severity is graded by FEV1 % predicted.
- **Reversibility:** an increase in FEV1 or FVC of at least 12% and 200 mL after bronchodilator is significant. It supports asthma but does not exclude COPD, and lack of response does not exclude asthma.
- **Restriction:** a low FVC with a normal ratio only suggests restriction; it must be confirmed by TLC below LLN on body plethysmography or gas dilution.
- **DLCO:** corrected for hemoglobin.

**Putting it together:**
- Obstruction + low DLCO: emphysema.
- Obstruction + normal or high DLCO: asthma (DLCO can be raised).
- Restriction + low DLCO: interstitial lung disease or pulmonary vascular loss with volume loss.
- Restriction + normal DLCO: extraparenchymal causes, such as obesity, kyphoscoliosis, neuromuscular weakness.
- Normal spirometry and volumes + isolated low DLCO: pulmonary vascular disease (PE, pulmonary hypertension), anemia, or early ILD or emphysema.
- Raised DLCO: alveolar hemorrhage, polycythemia, left-to-right shunt, asthma, obesity.

**Volumes:** emphysema shows hyperinflation (TLC raised) and air trapping (residual volume and RV/TLC raised).

**Flow-volume loops:** obstruction gives a concave ('scooped') expiratory limb. Restriction gives a narrow, tall loop. Upper airway lesions flatten the loop: a variable extrathoracic lesion (vocal cord dysfunction) flattens the inspiratory limb; a variable intrathoracic lesion flattens expiration; a fixed lesion (tracheal stenosis) flattens both.

In neuromuscular disease, measure maximal inspiratory pressure and supine versus upright FVC; a large supine drop suggests diaphragm weakness.
levels.phd:
Spirometric reference values are derived from healthy population cohorts; the Global Lung Function Initiative (GLI) equations use LMS modeling across ages 3-95 to define percentiles and z-scores. Expressing results as z-scores, with abnormal as below −1.645 (the fifth percentile), avoids age bias inherent in fixed ratios and percent-predicted thresholds. Race-specific equations were long used; the 2022-2023 ATS statements moved toward race-neutral (GLI Global) equations, debating whether race adjustments embedded social and environmental confounders as biology.

Physiologically, the forced expiratory maneuver interrogates flow limitation. Beyond the first fraction of expiration, flow is determined by lung elastic recoil and upstream resistance rather than effort, so the effort-independent portion is sensitive to small-airway and parenchymal disease. Yet FEV1 is relatively insensitive to the 'quiet zone' of small airways under 2 mm, where substantial disease can accumulate before spirometry changes. Tools probing this zone include oscillometry (resistance and reactance across frequencies), multiple-breath nitrogen washout (lung clearance index, sensitive in early cystic fibrosis) and parametric response mapping on paired inspiratory and expiratory CT.

DLCO reflects membrane conductance and capillary blood volume, separable by measuring at two oxygen concentrations (Roughton-Forster), or combining with nitric oxide transfer (DLNO), which is more membrane-weighted. KCO (DLCO per alveolar volume) helps separate loss of alveolar units (high KCO with low volume in pneumonectomy or extraparenchymal restriction) from intrinsic gas transfer defects (low KCO).

PRISm (preserved ratio impaired spirometry) describes reduced FEV1 with a normal ratio. It is heterogeneous, unstable over time, linked to obesity and cardiovascular risk, and a proportion progress to obstruction, challenging the binary obstructive-restrictive framework.

Finally, biological variability matters: between-session FEV1 changes under about 10% may be noise, influencing how trials and clinicians define meaningful decline.
levels.expert:
PFTs answer clinical questions; order and read them with a question in mind.

**Breathless patient, normal exam and X-ray:** full PFTs with DLCO. An isolated low DLCO should send you looking for pulmonary vascular disease, with echocardiography and assessment for chronic thromboembolism.

**Suspected asthma with normal spirometry:** asthma is variable, so a normal test between attacks does not exclude it. Options are serial peak flow variability, a bronchial challenge test (methacholine or mannitol, where a negative result makes current asthma unlikely), or fractional exhaled nitric oxide as a marker of type 2 airway inflammation.

**Pre-operative assessment:** before lung resection, calculate predicted postoperative FEV1 and DLCO from the number of segments removed; low predicted values trigger cardiopulmonary exercise testing. For other surgery, routine spirometry is not needed without symptoms.

**Neuromuscular disease:** this is where neurologists and neurosurgeons meet PFTs. In Guillain-Barré syndrome and myasthenic crisis, serial vital capacity and maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures track respiratory muscle failure; oxygen saturation stays normal until late, so it is a poor monitor. A falling vital capacity is the trigger to move toward the ICU and consider intubation. In ALS, a falling FVC or sniff nasal pressure guides when to start non-invasive ventilation.

**Common traps:**
- Calling restriction from spirometry alone without TLC.
- Missing a mixed defect (low ratio plus low TLC).
- Ignoring a flattened flow-volume loop, the clue to tracheal stenosis after prolonged intubation or tracheostomy, often misdiagnosed as 'asthma that does not respond'.
- Testing too soon after a respiratory infection.

Finally, pair numbers with function: the six-minute walk test with oxygen saturation tracks interstitial disease and pulmonary hypertension and can unmask exertional desaturation that resting tests miss.

keyPoints: Obstruction: low FEV1/FVC (below LLN or 0.70)
Restriction: confirmed by low TLC, ratio normal or high
Reversibility: FEV1 up ≥12% and ≥200 mL
Low DLCO: emphysema, ILD, pulmonary vascular disease
Flow-volume loops localize upper airway obstruction

test.q: FEV1 is:
choices: Air blown out in the first second
test.explain: Forced expiratory volume in 1 second.

test.q: An obstructive pattern shows:
choices: High TLC with normal ratio only
test.explain: FEV1 falls more than FVC, so the ratio drops.

test.q: Which disease classically gives a restrictive pattern?
test.explain: Scarring shrinks lung volumes; the ratio stays normal or high.

test.q: Restriction is confirmed by a low:
test.explain: Low FVC only suggests restriction; low TLC confirms it.

test.q: Significant bronchodilator reversibility, which supports asthma, is an FEV1 rise of at least:
test.explain: The standard threshold is ≥12% and ≥200 mL.

test.q: Obstruction with a LOW DLCO suggests:
test.explain: Emphysema destroys alveolar-capillary surface; asthma usually keeps DLCO normal.

test.q: Normal spirometry and lung volumes with an isolated low DLCO should raise concern for:
test.explain: Think pulmonary embolism or pulmonary hypertension (or anemia).

test.q: Restriction with NORMAL DLCO suggests a cause:
choices: Outside the lung tissue, such as obesity or muscle weakness
test.explain: Healthy alveoli in a small box: chest wall, pleura or muscle.

test.q: A flow-volume loop flattened in BOTH inspiration and expiration suggests:
choices: Fixed upper airway obstruction (e.g. tracheal stenosis)
test.explain: Fixed lesions limit flow in both directions.

test.q: The volume of a normal quiet breath is the ___ volume.
test.explain: Tidal volume is about half a litre in adults.

test.q: What is the main breathing test that measures FEV1 and FVC?
test.explain: Spirometry: forced exhalation into a spirometer.

test.q: Air remaining in the lungs after maximal exhalation is the ___ volume.
test.explain: Residual volume rises with air trapping in emphysema.

test.q: Asthma with normal spirometry between attacks can be confirmed with:
test.explain: Asthma is variable; challenge testing or peak-flow variability helps.

kidTest.q: In the lung test, you blow out:
choices: As hard and fast as you can
kidTest.explain: A big, fast blow is measured.

kidTest.q: Narrow lung tubes make air come out:
kidTest.explain: Like a skinny straw.

kidTest.q: Stiff lungs that will not stretch hold:
kidTest.explain: Like a balloon that will not blow up.

kidTest.q: The machine measures:
choices: How much air and how fast
kidTest.explain: Amount and speed of air.

kidTest.q: Before you blow out, you take the biggest ______ in you can.
kidTest.explain: Fill up first, then blow.

kidTest.q: This test helps doctors:
choices: Know what kind of lung trouble someone has
kidTest.explain: Different patterns mean different problems.

advancedTest.q: FEV1/FVC 0.82, FVC 60% predicted, TLC 95% predicted. Most accurate reading?
choices: Not restriction; consider poor effort, PRISm-like pattern or air trapping/early obstruction
advancedTest.explain: Normal TLC rules out restriction; a low FVC with preserved ratio has other explanations.

advancedTest.q: In Guillain-Barré syndrome, the best bedside monitor for impending respiratory failure is:
choices: Serial vital capacity and maximal inspiratory pressure
advancedTest.explain: Saturation stays normal until late; falling VC/MIP triggers ICU care.

advancedTest.q: Stridor and 'asthma not responding to inhalers' months after a prolonged intubation; loop flattened in both phases. Diagnosis?
advancedTest.explain: A fixed upper airway lesion flattens both limbs.

advancedTest.q: A raised DLCO is seen in:
advancedTest.explain: Blood in the alveoli takes up extra CO. Polycythemia and asthma can also raise it.
